name: The Newer Rules: Accessibility, Deepfakes, and State Law
title: The Newer Rules: Accessibility, Deepfakes, and State Law
answer: Three newer sets of rules now shape how schools handle AI: federal accessibility standards for district websites, apps and learning platforms, a federal law against publishing intimate images including AI-generated ones, and state laws that often go beyond federal requirements. Together they mean schools must update handbooks, reporting steps, staff training and AI policies, and in some states confirm their legal duties with counsel. These rules matter because they set concrete deadlines and obligations that sit alongside the privacy and safety practices schools already follow.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: This idea covers three newer categories of rules that apply to schools alongside existing privacy and safety requirements. The first is accessibility, where public school districts must bring their websites, online forms, learning platform content and apps up to the WCAG 2.1 Level AA standard. The second is deepfakes, where publishing intimate images of a person without consent, including AI-generated images, is a federal crime with heavier penalties when the victim is a minor. The third is state law, which frequently goes further than federal law by regulating education companies directly and issuing AI guidance for schools. The problem it solves is that schools may be unaware of obligations that arrive from several directions at once, and each one carries its own deadlines, reporting duties and policy updates.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, districts need to treat these three rule sets as workstreams rather than one-off tasks. For accessibility, districts in areas of 50,000 or more people have until April 26, 2027, and smaller districts until April 26, 2028, after an extension in April 2026, though that extension is being challenged in court. For deepfakes, schools should update handbooks, reporting steps and staff training so a targeted student knows exactly where to go, and covered platforms have had to remove reported images within 48 hours since May 19, 2026. For state law, most states have issued guidance on AI in schools, Ohio now requires every district to adopt an AI policy, and Texas districts should confirm their obligations with counsel under a governance law that took effect in January 2026. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, so the practical steps apply across a district rather than by year group.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels these as newer sets of rules and cites sources for each. For accessibility it cites THE Journal, 2026, for the WCAG 2.1 Level AA requirement, the April 2026 extension, the April 26, 2027 deadline for districts in areas of 50,000 or more people, the April 26, 2028 deadline for smaller districts, and the fact that the extension is being challenged in court. For deepfakes it cites Latham & Watkins, 2025, for the TAKE IT DOWN Act signed in May 2025, the federal crime of knowingly publishing intimate images without consent including AI-generated images, higher penalties when the victim is a minor, and the 48-hour removal requirement for covered platforms since May 19, 2026. For state law it cites ManagedMethods, n.d., for at least 40 states having passed student privacy laws by 2019 and many regulating education companies directly following California's model, and Texas Legislature, 2025, for Texas's AI governance law taking effect in January 2026. The text also states that most states have issued guidance on AI in schools and that Ohio now requires every district to adopt an AI policy.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets out several limits and cautions. The accessibility extension is being challenged in court, so the deadlines may not hold as stated. Texas districts are told to confirm their obligations with counsel because the state's AI governance law defines covered government entities broadly enough to include school districts. The deepfake rules place duties on covered platforms to remove reported images within 48 hours, while schools are directed to update handbooks, reporting steps and staff training so a targeted student knows where to go. Decisions about how to interpret state law, what an AI policy should contain, and how to confirm obligations remain with district leaders and their counsel rather than with any automated tool. Nothing in the text removes the need for human judgement about a specific district's circumstances.
